text:
🇲🇽🏭 <u>MEXICAN INDUSTRY POSTS ITS BEST GROWTH IN 3 YEARS</u>

Mexico's industrial output rose 2.42% year-on-year in July — its strongest reading in 33 months, according to INEGI — driven by a 6.66% jump in construction and manufacturing returning to growth (+1.33%) after 12 straight months of contraction. Manufacturing of computer and electronic equipment surged 13.5%, its best in 43 months.

🇲🇽🏥 <u>PUEBLA'S MOBILE HOSPITAL BRINGS FREE SURGERY TO THE POOR</u>

Puebla's new "5 de Mayo" itinerant hospital travels to isolated communities performing cataract, pterygium, hernia and other surgeries at no cost — its 210 m² operating room, filtering 99.97% of bacteria, is billed as the largest in Latin America. Governor Alejandro Armenta opened it as healthcare that goes to the people; one patient from Teziutlán, after cataract surgery: "they made our dream to see again come true." A second mobile hospital is already budgeted for next year.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>PRI'S BOSS LOCKS IN POWER TO 2032</u>

Alejandro "Alito" Moreno rewrote the PRI's statutes to allow indefinite reelection, securing his grip on the party — and its roughly 800 million pesos a year in public financing from the INE — until 2032, all while under multiple corruption probes. In August 2026 two of his associates were arrested over an alleged 36-million-peso diversion via fake invoices. This is the man caught on tape saying journalists shouldn't be shot — "you have to starve them to death."

🔥🇲🇽 <u>FOBAPROA'S ARCHITECT STILL CASHES A LIFETIME CHECK</u>

Ernesto Zedillo — the president who in 1997 turned private bankers' losses into public debt through Fobaproa — still draws a 149,203-peso monthly lifetime pension from Banxico (about 1.8 million a year), even after AMLO scrapped ex-presidents' pensions. Finance Secretary Edgar Amador: "we've paid nearly 1.6 trillion pesos over the years and not a single peso of principal has been paid." The bailout's net liabilities still stood at 1.01 trillion pesos in June 2026.

🇲🇽🐄 <u>CATTLE EXPORTS TO THE US REOPEN</u>

Shut since November 2024 over the screwworm (gusano barrenador) outbreak, the San Jerónimo–Santa Teresa crossing reopens September 24 for Chihuahua cattle bound for the US — starting at about 800 head the first week and scaling to 1,500 a day by the fourth. Before the closure Chihuahua moved some 500,000 head north a year; Senasica retooled its quarantine station to USDA standards and won reauthorization from Washington.

🇲🇽📵 <u>MEXICO BANS PHONES IN THE CLASSROOM</u>

From October, cellphone use is restricted for the entire school day in every public primary and secondary school in Mexico — a national accord approved unanimously by the education authorities of all 32 states (Conaedu). SEP secretary Mario Delgado frames it around protecting children's and adolescents' mental health and giving classrooms back to learning.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>MEXICO SHIPS THE AI BOOM, KEEPS THE CRUMBS</u>

Mexico exported 85.4 billion dollars in computer equipment in 2025 — up 144.8%, feeding the US AI data-center boom. But foreign investment in actually building that gear was just 508 million dollars across an entire decade (2016–2025), and fell 16.1% in the first half of 2026, per El Economista. The chips come from Asia, the value books abroad, Mexico assembles. Tech sovereignty won't arrive by waiting on foreign capital.

🇲🇽📉 <u>GUANAJUATO'S HOMICIDES CRASH 75%</u>

Mexico's deadliest state is turning: Guanajuato's daily homicide average fell 75% — from 12.7 in February 2025 to 3.2 in August 2026 — with high-impact crimes down 43% and 10,699 people detained since October 2024, Sheinbaum reported from Irapuato. The state could close 2026 with its fewest killings in eight years, under a PAN governor and a Morena president who set politics aside.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>3,436 MORE TROOPS INTO SINALOA</u>

Mexico's federal Security Cabinet — Harfuch, Defense, Navy and the National Guard — deployed 3,436 additional troops to Mazatlán and its highways, on top of the 20,000-plus federal forces already in Sinaloa. The reinforcement: 1,600 Army, 1,000 Navy, 836 police and 100 special forces, agreed with the state's interim governor.

🇲🇽🕊️ <u>190,000 SIGNATURES FOR A DIGNIFIED DEATH</u>

Mexico's Human Rights Commission (CNDH) formally received "Ley Trasciende," a citizen initiative for the right to end life without suffering for the terminally and chronically ill — backed by roughly 190,000 signatures gathered by the Muerte Digna ¡Ya! coalition. CNDH president Rosario Piedra pledged to keep "open spaces for listening, dialogue and participation."
